name: Sidney

facts.text: Sidney's Tree Preservation Bylaw No. 2138 protects listed native species, replacement trees, trees required by a development permit, trees in environmental development permit areas, Town trees and any tree over 60 cm in diameter.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Preservation Bylaw - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Any tree having a diameter greater than 60 cm
facts.note: V2: confirmed on the live page; the excerpt is now verbatim (capital A).

facts.text: Under Bylaw No. 2138, Douglas-fir, bigleaf maple, grand fir and western redcedar are protected once they are 1.2 m tall. Arbutus, cascara, Garry oak, Pacific dogwood, seaside juniper, shore pine and western yew are protected from 3 cm in diameter, measured 1.4 m above the ground.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Preservation Bylaw No. 2138 (consolidated) - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Western Redcedar (Thuja plicata) trees with a height of 1.2 metres or more, and Arbutus (Arbutus menziesii), Cascara (Rhamnus purshiana), Garry Oak (Quercus garryana)
facts.note: V2: new, from the bylaw's definitions (s.3). The list continues verbatim: 'Pacific Dogwood (Cornus nuttallii), Seaside Juniper (Juniperus maritima), Shore Pine (Pinus contorta var. contorta) and Western Yew (Taxus brevifolia) Trees with a Diameter of 3 cm or more.' Section 5.1 sets the measuring point at 1.4 m. This closes the R1b gap on the species list.

facts.text: Without a permit, Sidney allows up to 20% of a protected tree's crown to be pruned in a season, to ISA or ASCA standards, for the tree's health. Cutting any branch, stem or root over 5 cm in diameter (over 2.5 cm for arbutus, Pacific dogwood and Garry oak) needs a Tree Permit, and fill, materials or structures may not go inside a protected tree's drip line.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Preservation Bylaw No. 2138 (consolidated) - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: up to 20% of Crown of a Protected Tree during a season for the purpose of maintaining or improving the health of the Tree.
facts.note: V2: new, from sections 6.3-6.5 of the bylaw. 'Protected Root Zone' is defined as the area within the drip line (s.3), and s.6.5(b) bars placing fill, building materials, asphalt or structures there.

facts.text: On private land, removing, extensively pruning or topping a protected tree may need a Tree Removal Permit. The Town asks owners to call the Parks Department (250-656-1034) to talk to Sidney's arborist before starting.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Preservation Bylaw - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: To remove, extensively prune, or top an existing tree located on private property, you may require a Tree Removal Permit.
facts.note: V2: confirmed. The Tree Removal and Pruning Permits page (https://www.sidney.ca/services/trees/tree-removal-and-pruning-permits/) adds, verbatim: 'should contact the Parks Department at 250-656-1034 or by email at engineeringservices@sidney.ca to discuss with Sidney’s Arborist before you begin.'

facts.text: Sidney's tree permit application covers pruning and removal of protected trees. Every protected tree removed needs replacement trees and a refundable per-tree deposit, returned if the new trees are healthy after two years; if they are not planted on site, the Town plants them on Town land and charges a per-tree fee in lieu.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Permit Application (Town of Sidney)
facts.excerpt: This deposit will be returned if the trees are healthy after 2 years, upon approval by the Town Arborist.
facts.note: V2: the old 2025_REV PDF now returns 404; the current form is linked from the Tree Removal and Pruning Permits page. Correction: the form shows that the per-tree amount is BOTH a refundable deposit (replacements planted on site) and a fee in lieu (Town plants elsewhere). The form also lists permit fees. CONTRACT: no $ amounts in content, so do not publish the figures.

facts.text: Sidney's tree permit application requires that tree removal and pruning be done by a certified arborist hired by the applicant.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Permit Application (Town of Sidney)
facts.excerpt: Tree removal and pruning must be done by a certified arborist contracted by the applicant.
facts.note: V2: new. The bylaw defines Certified Arborist as one certified by the ISA or the American Society of Consulting Arborists (s.3). RNC must not claim arborist credentials unless [CERTIFICATIONS] confirms them.

facts.text: Properties in Sidney's Environmentally Sensitive Area development permit areas, which take in creeks, shorelines and upland forest, need an approved development permit before any construction or landscaping that significantly affects the land or water.
facts.sourceTitle: Environmentally Sensitive Areas - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Properties within an Environmentally Sensitive Area DPA require an approved Development Permit prior to any construction or landscaping that has a significant impact on the land or water.
facts.note: V2: confirmed. The old excerpt was paraphrased; it is now verbatim.

facts.text: In Sidney's environmentally sensitive areas, gardening and yard maintenance within an existing landscaped area is among the common exempt activities. Changes to landscaping that alter the land can need a development permit, so the Town suggests talking to staff early.
facts.sourceTitle: Environmentally Sensitive Areas - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: gardening and yard maintenance within an existing landscaped area
facts.note: V2: new, from the FAQ 'When would a Development Permit in an environmentally sensitive area be required?' Same page, verbatim: 'This can include new construction, additions/alterations to the exterior of a building, structure, or fencing, and changes to landscaping.'

facts.text: Reay Creek and Mermaid Creek provide fish habitat and help filter stormwater, so lots next to them may also fall under the Province's riparian rules.
facts.sourceTitle: Environmentally Sensitive Areas - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: properties around Mermaid Creek and Reay Creek may be subject to the Province’s Riparian Areas Protection Regulation.
facts.note: V2: confirmed; the excerpt is now verbatim. Same page: 'Streams like Reay Creek or Mermaid Creek can provide many benefits, such as contributing to fish habitat and providing important storm water services'.

facts.text: Sidney's marine-shoreline environmentally sensitive area takes in already-developed waterfront lots, many with older concrete seawalls. When those lots are rebuilt, the guidelines look to protect or restore natural shoreline and vegetation, keep building back from the high-water mark, or use naturalized approaches such as Green Shores.
facts.sourceTitle: Environmentally Sensitive Areas - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: protect or restore natural shoreline and vegetation, avoid construction that is too close to the high water mark, or incorporate naturalized solutions, such as GreenShores
facts.note: V2: new, from the FAQ 'Why are already-developed areas along the marine shoreline included in ESAs?' The same FAQ section names upland areas north of Allbay Road and on the Beaufort Peninsula as among 'Sidney’s last remaining stands of coastal Douglas fir trees'.

facts.text: Sidney's 2025 flood mapping treats the first 30 m inland from the shoreline as a wave effect zone, the land most exposed to wave run-up and spray. Plants and features there face salt and storm exposure. The mapped flood construction levels are not yet regulatory; the Town's interim policy still applies.
facts.sourceTitle: Sea Level Rise - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Land within 30 meters of the shoreline is most exposed to wave run-up and spray.
facts.note: V2: new; this closes the R1b salt-spray/exposure gap from an official page. Same page, verbatim: 'the FCLs shown on the maps are not yet regulatory requirements'. 'Salt exposure for plants' is our wording; the Town says 'wave run-up and spray'.

facts.text: Under Sidney's Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw No. 1738 (2002), owners keep the boulevard next to their property neat and tidy and the grass cut. The Town can deem a boulevard unsightly or a hazard, direct the owner in writing to maintain it, and if the owner does not, do the work at the owner's expense.
facts.sourceTitle: Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw No. 1738 (Town of Sidney)
facts.excerpt: All owners of real property shall maintain the boulevard in a neat and tidy condition and shall keep the grass cut on all boulevards that abut a street
facts.note: V2: confirmed. The old excerpt was paraphrased; it is now verbatim. The bare host sidney.ca was refused by the network, but the same file loads on www.sidney.ca. Bylaw dated 2002, and no amendments were found on the file. It states an hourly charge; CONTRACT: no $ amounts.

facts.text: Wood burning is not allowed in Sidney. Residential waste, construction-site, demolition, land-clearing and beach fires are prohibited; propane and charcoal fire pits are permitted.
facts.sourceTitle: Fire Services - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Wood burning within the Town of Sidney is not permitted.
facts.note: V2: sidney.ca/?p=2028 now redirects to the Fire Services page. Same FAQ, verbatim: 'Residential waste, construction site, demolition site, land-clearing and beach fire burning are prohibited. Propane and charcoal fire pits are permitted.' The bylaw is the Fire Department Service Level Establishment and Fire Regulation Bylaw (file 2087). Correction: removed 'prunings go to yard-waste collection instead', which was our inference, not the Town's wording.

facts.text: Sidney's contractor collects yard and garden waste at the curb twice a month. Each household may set out up to three lidless rigid cans or three kraft-paper yard bags of up to 80 L and 20 kg each, and branches must be under 3 inches in diameter, in bundles up to 3 ft long. There is no yard-waste pickup for commercial units.
facts.sourceTitle: Yard & Garden Waste - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Households may put out up to three rigid garbage cans without lids or three compostable craft paper yard waste bags, with a maximum volume of 80L and 20kg (44lbs) each.
facts.note: V2: sidney.ca/?p=1994 redirects here. Confirmed; added the three-container limit and branch size. Bylaw 2259 (https://www.sidney.ca/wp-content/uploads/2259-Collection-and-Disposal-of-Refuse.pdf) s.9, verbatim: 'Yard waste pickup is not available for commercial units.' Note: the page and the bylaw also say 'monthly' in one place, against 'twice per month' / 'twice monthly' elsewhere; we use twice monthly.

facts.text: Sidney's curbside yard-waste collection will not take morning glory, blackberry, wild mustard, ox-eye daisy, wild carrot, couch grass, poison hemlock or any invasive plant species, so invasive clearings need separate disposal.
facts.sourceTitle: Yard & Garden Waste - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: Morning glory, blackberry, wild mustard, ox-eye daisy, wild carrot, couch grass, poison hemlock, and all invasive plant species are unacceptable.
facts.note: V2: new. See the shared regional fact regional-crd-invasive-disposal for Hartland Landfill disposal.

facts.text: Sidney gets its water from the CRD system fed by Sooke Lake, and the Town notes that the CRD's Stage 1 watering schedule applies every year from May 1 to September 30.
facts.sourceTitle: Water - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: The Town receives water from the Capital Regional District (CRD) trunk distribution system from Sooke Lake.
facts.note: V2: new; closes the R1b gap 'confirm the CRD water conservation bylaw applies to Sidney'. Same page, verbatim: 'The CRD sets water restrictions for our region. Stage 1 Watering Schedule is in effect May 1 through September 30 every year'.

facts.text: Sidney has a Community Wildfire Resiliency Plan (2024) supporting its FireSmart program, and the Fire Department points residents to the FireSmart BC Landscaping Guide.
facts.sourceTitle: Wildfire Resiliency - Town of Sidney
facts.excerpt: The Town of Sidney has developed a Community Wildfire Resiliency Plan (CWRP) for Sidney to guide the Town’s efforts to prevent and respond to potential wildfires.
facts.note: V2: new. The plan PDF is Community-Wildfire-Resiliency-Plan-2024.pdf (not read). The page links FireSmart BC's Landscaping Guide.

facts.text: CRD Stage 1 watering rules (Water Conservation Bylaw No. 4099) run May 1 to September 30 every year for properties on the Regional Water Supply System: lawns may be watered two days a week by address (even: Wednesday and Saturday; odd: Thursday and Sunday), 4-10 am or 7-10 pm by any method, or 12:01-10 am or 7-10 pm with timed/automatic irrigation. Trees, shrubs, flowers and vegetable gardens may be sprinkled any day 4-10 am or 7-10 pm, and hand watering or micro/drip irrigation is allowed any day, any time. Strata and other multi-unit complexes use the complex's street address. New sod and newly seeded lawns need no permit and have a temporary schedule.
facts.sourceTitle: Regional Watering Schedule - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: Stage 1 Watering Schedule of the Water Conservation Bylaw No. 4099 for the Regional Water Supply System is in effect May 1 through September 30 every year.
facts.note: V2: verified on the live CRD page (www.crd.ca/node/4919 redirects here). Corrections: added the separate timed/automatic irrigation window (12:01-10 am or 7-10 pm), the any-day rules for trees, shrubs and gardens, the multi-unit address rule and the bylaw number. Shared regional block, not municipality-specific; R1a files use the id 'crd-watering-stage1' for the same rule, so the integrator should merge the two ids.

facts.text: The CRD's Juan de Fuca Water Distribution System supplies drinking water to Colwood, Langford, Metchosin, View Royal, Sooke, parts of Highlands and East Sooke; the Saanich Peninsula Water Distribution System supplies Central Saanich, Sidney and North Saanich. Properties not connected (for example on private wells) are outside the CRD watering schedule.
facts.sourceTitle: Drinking Water Systems - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: The Juan de Fuca Water Distribution System provides drinking water to Colwood, Langford, Metchosin, View Royal, Sooke, parts of Highlands and electoral area East Sooke.
facts.note: V2: new shared regional fact. Same page, verbatim: 'The Saanich Peninsula Water Distribution System provides drinking water to Central Saanich, Sidney and North Saanich.' The last sentence (unconnected properties are outside the schedule) follows from the watering page, which says Bylaw 4099 applies to customers of the Regional Water Supply System.

facts.text: Invasive plants can be taken to Hartland Landfill in bags marked 'Invasive Species' or in covered loads; knotweed needs a controlled waste permit and must not go to municipal yard-waste drop-offs. The CRD's Regional Invasive Species Program lists priority species including giant hogweed, knotweed, gorse, poison hemlock, shiny geranium and yellow toadflax.
facts.sourceTitle: Invasive Species - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: Invasive species can be disposed of at Hartland Landfill. They must be in bags marked “Invasive Species” or in covered loads.
facts.note: V2: new shared regional fact; it confirms the CRD invasive-species note already used in content/areas/*.json. Same page, verbatim: 'Knotweed species disposal requires a controlled waste permit (reduced fee)' and 'Note: Knotweed species must not be disposed of at these locations.'

facts.text: B.C.'s riparian rules (the Riparian Areas Protection Regulation, formerly the Riparian Areas Regulation) apply across the Capital Regional District except the City of Victoria and Esquimalt. Residential, commercial or industrial work within 30 m of a fish-bearing stream, lake, wetland or ditch, including removing or altering plants and disturbing soil, can need a Qualified Environmental Professional's assessment; each local government sets how it applies through permit areas or bylaws. Amendments to the regulation take effect January 1, 2027.
facts.sourceTitle: Riparian Areas Regulation brochure (Province of B.C., 2016)
facts.excerpt: within 30 metres of a watercourse, even if that watercourse is not on your property,
facts.note: V2: the 30 m figure is not on the RAPR web page itself, so the source is now the provincial brochure. Brochure, verbatim: the activities listed include 'Removing or altering plants' and 'Disturbing soils'. Regulation page (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/plants-animals-ecosystems/fish/aquatic-habitat-management/riparian-areas-regulation), verbatim: 'Amendments to RAPR come into effect on January 1, 2027.' Citizen resources page (.../riparian-areas-regulation/citizen-resources), verbatim: 'Capital (except City of Victoria and Esquimalt)'. The 2016 guidebook adds that the rules do not apply to marine or estuarine shorelines. The brochure predates the 2019 rename and the 2027 amendments, so re-check after January 1, 2027.

facts.text: Section 34 of B.C.'s Wildlife Act makes it an offence to take, injure, molest or destroy a bird or its egg, the nest of an eagle, peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon, osprey, heron or burrowing owl (protected even when not in use), or any other bird's nest while it holds a bird or egg. Trees are therefore checked for nests before felling or heavy pruning, especially in spring and summer.
facts.sourceTitle: Migratory Birds and Breeding Birds: Federal and Provincial Legislation (BC Timber Sales, March 2024)
facts.excerpt: possesses, takes, injures, molests or destroys: a) A bird or its egg, b) The nest of an eagle, peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon, osprey, heron or burrowing owl
facts.note: V2: the earlier source (www2.gov.bc.ca .../environmental-regulatory-compliance/wildlife) now returns 404, so the source is now this provincial guidance sheet, which quotes section 34. Same sheet, verbatim: 'c) The nest of a bird not referred to in paragraph (b) when the nest is occupied by a bird or its egg.' It also says inactive nests of listed species 'have regulatory protection'. Correction: the species list is now exact (peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon and burrowing owl added; 'some other nests' removed).

gaps: Deer: no Town of Sidney deer program found on the pages read; the Sidney Island deer project is a different place and must not be used.
Shoal Harbour Migratory Bird Sanctuary: the ESA page mentions 'the Migratory Bird Sanctuary' without naming it; the federal page (canada.ca) is outside this session's network.
Significant Tree List (https://www.sidney.ca/services/trees/significant-tree-list/) and the 2024 CWRP PDF were not read.
